name: Atropine
addictionPotential: not typically considered addictive due to unpleasant effects at active doses
toxicities: Anticholinergic toxicity: hyperthermia, tachycardia, delirium, seizures, respiratory depression, coma. Relatively low LD50 in humans.
summary: Atropine is a tropane alkaloid and anticholinergic agent found in plants of the Solanaceae family (including Datura). It acts as a competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Medically used for bradycardia, as an antisialagogue, and as an antidote for organophosphate poisoning. At high doses it produces anticholinergic delirium.
effectsSummary: Anticholinergic syndrome: dry mouth, blurred vision, photophobia, dilated pupils, urinary retention, constipation, tachycardia, flushing, hyperthermia. At delirium doses: confusion, agitation, hallucinations, amnesia.
dosageRemark: Medical doses: 0.4-1mg IV/IM. Toxic symptoms begin above 2mg. Severe toxicity above 10mg. The delirium threshold varies widely between individuals.
generalRisks: Peripheral anticholinergic effects even at low doses. Central anticholinergic syndrome at higher doses: confusion, agitation, hallucinations, coma. Hyperthermia risk in hot environments.
longtermRisks: Chronic use not recommended due to anticholinergic burden. Long-term anticholinergic use associated with increased dementia risk.
saferUse: Avoid in hot environments due to hyperthermia risk
Do not combine with other anticholinergics
metabolism: The cited evidence is for 1% w/v atropine eye drops, with metabolic data from intravenous [3H] atropine sulphate in a single healthy subject. Five drug-related peaks were detected in that subject's urine: unchanged drug plus an enantiomer later identified as biologically inactive made up 57% of total radioactivity, noratropine (24%) and atropine-A-oxide (15%) were the main metabolites, and tropin (2%) and tropic acid (3%) were minor metabolites. No glucuronide or sulfate conjugates appeared in human urine. About 75% of total radioactivity was excreted in urine within 13 hours of intravenous administration. By the ocular route, systemic bioavailability of a 30 microlitre dose ranged from 19% to 95% (mean about 63.5%) and the terminal half-life was comparable to intravenous dosing (2.97 h intravenous vs 2.45 h topical), so ocular administration did not change elimination kinetics.
